title: Share even the last bite
hookLine: if beings knew the result of giving, they would not eat without sharing
last: PULL IT UP BY THE ROOT.

lines: THREE SMALL WORDS: AS I KNOW.
cards: Two kids, one cookie left. Watch what happens. Usually it's a negotiation: who had more, who's bigger, who asked first.
And sometimes, rarely, one of them just breaks it and hands over half without being asked. Grown-ups do the same math with bigger things.
On day one hundred thirty-four you met this teaching from the Itivuttaka: if people knew, they'd share. Today, read it closer, and listen for three small words in the middle of it: as I know.

teach.h: IF BEINGS KNEW, AS I KNOW.

teach.b: If beings knew, as I know, the result of giving and sharing, dana and samvibhaga, they would not eat without having given, and the stain of stinginess would not take hold of their minds.
Even if it were their last bite, their last mouthful, they would not eat without sharing it, if there were someone to receive it.
But because beings don't know, as I know, they eat without having given, and the stain of stinginess takes hold. Now the phrase: as I know. The Buddha isn't saying be nicer.
He's saying the problem is not knowing. If you could really see what giving does, to the receiver and to the giver, you wouldn't need to be told; you'd just do it, the way you'd step out of the rain.
Stinginess, in this teaching, is a kind of blindness, and the word for it is a stain, something that clouds the mind.

teach.h: IF THERE WERE SOMEONE TO RECEIVE.
teach.b: Notice the small realism at the end: if there were someone to receive it. Nobody is asked to throw food away to prove a point. It's about the moment when there's someone in front of you.
And notice the scale. Not a fortune. A mouthful, about as small as a gift can be.
Even there, the hand can open.

how: In many Buddhist homes a portion of food is set aside or offered before eating, and giving food to monks, neighbors and those in need is among the most common daily acts of generosity.

o: a meal offered to the monks

games.q: share even the last bite: tap the pairs.
p: if there were someone to receive

s: Itivuttaka 26 says people are stingy because they're bad
it says they don't know the result of giving, as the Buddha knows it.
the teaching says some would share even their last mouthful
if they knew the result of giving, and someone were there to receive.
the stain of stinginess takes hold of the mind when people don't know.

games.q: you're down to your last bite, and someone is sitting next to you with nothing. according to Itivuttaka 26, what would you do if you truly knew the result of giving?
games.why: the teaching says that if beings knew as the Buddha knows, they wouldn't eat even the last bite without sharing it, if someone were there to receive.

practice: Remember a time someone shared food with you when they didn't have much, a grandparent, a stranger, a friend splitting a sandwich, and feel what it did for you then.
Then picture your next meal, who will be near you, and yourself offering them something from your plate, and simply enjoy the picture.

wordCard.voice: Samvibhaga, sharing. Itivuttaka 26: if beings knew, as the Buddha knows, the result of giving, they'd share even their last mouthful. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali samvibhaga: sharing, dividing out. Itivuttaka 26 speaks of the fruit of dana and samvibhaga, giving and sharing.

carryVoice: Your line: notice who it feeds. The trouble, this teaching says, is not knowing. Day six hundred twenty-eight, done.
